title: One Vocabulary, Two Operators
summary: The whitepaper in plain words: one closed list of actions that a human and an AI operate identically through one door, with the AI's hand shown in the surface. This lesson covers the idea, how it is built, who holds which piece, the claim I make and do not make, and what I have not earned.

stops.title: The AI that pretends to be a person

beats.quote: the model perceives pixels, the DOM, or the accessibility tree and emits low-level input
beats.text: It is the most academic thing I have written, full of citations, and I am going to say it in plain words. If you want the references, they are all in the note. The usual answer is imitation. The model looks at the screen, or the page structure, or the accessibility tree, and then it clicks and types the way a person would, because somebody asked it to in a chat. That is a GUI agent. It is powerful and it is general. It is also indirect. The model is reverse-engineering an interface that was built for eyes and hands, and the human is reduced to giving instructions and watching.

beats.quote: the AI has no affordance a person lacks
beats.text: I describe the inverse. In GRAIN, which is my design system, the interface publishes one small, closed list of actions. The application writes that list, and the AI cannot add to it. A human click and an AI decision turn into the same thing, which I call an Intent. Both go through one door, a single endpoint, and both come back as updates to the page. There is no side channel where the AI reaches into the page on its own. The AI has no move that a person lacks.

beats.quote: surface shows the AI's hand
beats.text: The second half is disclosure. Most systems tell you an AI was involved with a chat log, or a badge, or a label off to the side. I put the AI's hand in the surface itself. Text the AI wrote is set in a degraded grade of the type. A control the AI is touching gets a dashed edge. And the mark stays after the action is done. Human work settles clean. AI work keeps its grain. The sentence the whole paper hangs on is this. Every surface can be addressed and operated by both a human and an AI through one shared vocabulary, and the AI's presence is a visible signal.

beats.quote: A crowded road is evidence of a real destination.
beats.text: And because one writer arbitrates every change, the person has no shortcut either. Equal footing runs both ways, and it's built into the structure rather than bolted on as a stop button. I read a crowded road as a sign the destination is real. The paper's job is to name the spot on that road nobody has reached yet, and to say honestly which neighbor holds which piece. The idea that a person learns by watching is a hypothesis about people. I have not tested it.

runes.quote: the AI has no affordance a person lacks
A crowded road is evidence of a real destination.
the operator holds no direct-write shortcut either

stops.trial: Pick one AI tool you use that acts on a page or an app. Write down, in two sentences, whether it imitates your clicks or calls actions the app defines, and how it tells you what it did.
digest: Most AI agents imitate a person clicking.
GRAIN gives a human and an AI one closed list of actions and one door.
The AI's hand shows in the surface, and the limits are stated up front.

stops.title: One door, one writer

beats.quote: it cannot drift from the UI because
beats.text: Here is how the thing is actually put together. There are five parts, and I'll take them one at a time. First, two registries. One is surfaces. A surface is a stable, meaningful address on the page, a name rather than a CSS selector. The other is actions, a closed and typed list of what can be done. What you can operate is exactly those two lists multiplied together, and that gets written out as a manifest the machine can read. The manifest is harvested from the component tree, so it can't drift from the UI. It is a projection of the UI.

beats.quote: door, one writer: CRUD is
beats.text: The usual way a web app works is create, read, update and delete, straight to the data. I turned that around. The UI does no direct writes at all. When you click something, that becomes an Intent sent to one endpoint, exactly like an AI decision does. One layer checks the surface and the action against the registry and hands it to the one writer, which I call the reasoner. Only the reasoner can change state, and it pushes the result back. So neither operator has a privileged path. The human does not reach into the database any more than the AI reaches into the page.

beats.quote: provenance is permanent, not a loading state
beats.text: Fourth, the grade as a signal, and it is on every surface, not only type. Two separate attributes drive it. One is provenance, whether the AI or a human made this. The other is liveness, whether it is still in transit or committed. Text shows the AI as a degraded font grade. A button gets a dashed edge and a block caret while it is acting. When an AI action commits, the liveness settles, but the grade stays grain. That is provenance, and it is permanent, not a loading state. Disclosure belongs to the surface. It is never a separate badge.

beats.quote: A stream of pixel-clicks cannot be narrated meaningfully
beats.text: Fifth, the action log. Because every action is a named verb, the AI's activity can be narrated as a running feed of those verbs. You see it read, type, write, revise and commit, instead of watching a spinner. You can't narrate a stream of pixel clicks in any useful way. A closed vocabulary you can.

runes.quote: it cannot drift from the UI because
provenance is permanent, not a loading state
A stream of pixel-clicks cannot be narrated meaningfully

stops.trial: Take one screen of an app you know. List three surfaces on it by a plain name and three actions a person can take there. You have just drafted a tiny vocabulary.
digest: Two lists define what can be operated, and the manifest of them is harvested from the UI itself.
A human and an AI both send Intents through one door to one writer.
The AI's mark stays after the action commits.

stops.title: Who already holds which piece

beats.quote: three axes are the three
beats.text: I'll walk the map out loud and leave the citations on the page. The table has three columns that matter. Is the human and the AI on one shared vocabulary? Is there one writer and one door? And is there a signal that the AI was here? My point is that every cluster of prior work holds some of those, and only this work holds all three at once.

beats.quote: agents connect to user-facing apps
beats.text: Start with the agent and UI protocols, AG-UI, MCP-UI, MCP Apps and Google's A2UI. They're my closest industry neighbors. They share my instinct that the AI must not change the page directly. But each of them is a negotiation between an agent and an app, and the two sides are not the same. None of them sends a human click and an AI decision through one identical closed vocabulary. So no back channel from the AI is not my novelty. Lots of people have it.

beats.quote: an agent's completed work is visually indistinguishable from a human's
beats.text: Then the closest contemporary, Builder.io's Agent-Native, announced in May 2026. Its pitch is that every action the agent can take is also a button in the UI, and every button runs the same logic the agent uses. That is my symmetry claim, shipped by someone else. As of mid-2026 I can't call symmetry novel on its own, and I cite them as proof the idea is real and wanted. And the decisive one: they have no provenance surface. An agent's finished work looks exactly like a human's. So my claim now rests on the grade being tied to the same door that enforces the symmetry.

beats.quote: It is the concept; ours is the contract.
beats.text: There is an academic paper called Terminal Is All You Need that argues the terminal already puts human and agent in the same medium. I agree with the instinct. But the terminal's vocabulary is open text, there's no single writer, and what the agent did scrolls away. It is the concept. Mine is the contract. My narrower claim is the mark in the operable surface itself, persistent, and coupled to the action system. I do not claim it is better. Whether people read it correctly is open.

runes.quote: an agent's completed work is visually indistinguishable from a human's
It is the concept; ours is the contract.
so the bare concept of in-surface disclosure is not ours either

stops.trial: Draw the three columns from this stop on paper: shared vocabulary, one door, AI signal. Place two AI tools you know in it and mark which columns each fills.
digest: Every neighbor holds some of the three properties.
Agent-Native holds two and has no provenance surface.
The claim is the conjunction, and the bare ideas are named as borrowed.

stops.title: A synthesis and an existence proof

beats.quote: We do not claim a new capability
beats.text: It is an architectural synthesis and a working existence proof. I do not claim a new capability, and I don't need one. The value is the specific combination, built and running. There are three properties. One is symmetry. A human click and an AI decision become the identical Intent, over one closed vocabulary the application writes. Not generic device input, and not trees the agent proposes. Two is the single-writer door. One endpoint, no privileged path from the AI into the page, enforced as a rule of the architecture. That makes what the AI may do literally equal to what the UI offers. Three is provenance as grade. The AI's presence shows in the surface it produced or touched, and it is stamped at the same door that admits the action.

beats.quote: a position converged upon from independent directions is a real position
beats.text: And I have to be honest that the map moved under me. My first adversarial search, in July 2026, found nothing that ran a human and an AI through one closed vocabulary. A second sweep days later found exactly one, Agent-Native, with the first two properties and no provenance at all. So I narrowed the claim. Symmetry and the single writer are no longer new on their own. The claim rests on the full combination, where the grade is not decoration but is enforced by the door. I read that as validation, not erosion. When people arrive at the same position from different directions, the position is real.

beats.quote: small language model runs entirely
beats.text: When I first drafted this, the reasoner behind the model seam was a scripted stub. Now a small language model runs entirely in the browser, on WebLLM, with no server, on your own hardware. It reads the same vocabulary the human uses and sends Intents through the same door. It drives a subset end to end, navigation and choices, and its presence shows as grade, the way the architecture requires. And here are the limits, in the same breath. The model is small. Its command of the full vocabulary is unproven. This shows the thing is feasible. It doesn't measure whether the manifest is enough as a general instruction set, and it's not a study of any benefit.

beats.quote: we state them as hypotheses, not results
beats.text: The benefits are hypotheses. There are three. Using the AI through the same vocabulary gives people better expectations and more control than a chat agent working behind the scenes. The grade is noticed and read correctly at least as well as a badge, including for low-vision users. And watching the AI work step by step helps people learn the task. Writing that design costs nothing. Running it is the real work, and I haven't.

runes.quote: We do not claim a new capability
a position converged upon from independent directions is a real position
we state them as hypotheses, not results

stops.trial: Write one of the three hypotheses as a test you could run with two friends in ten minutes: what they do, and what you would measure.
digest: The claim is three properties together, not a new capability.
A small live model now drives a narrow slice through the door.
Every benefit is still a hypothesis waiting on a user study.

stops.title: What I have not earned yet

beats.quote: Positioning must be dated, not absolute.
beats.text: The paper has a section on limits and threats, and I'd rather you heard it from me than found it. First, what is built. The reference implementation enforces the door, the registry check and the grade, with unit, integration and conformance tests, for the human operator. Provenance is stamped on the server and tested against spoofing. And two older direct-write routes still exist in the demo app. They predate the door and are being retired into the documented ownership seam. Second, the ground moves fast. The agent and UI protocols are months old. Benchmarks age in weeks. So every claim about where I stand has to carry a date.

beats.quote: operating it, within the scope
beats.text: Third, vendor framing. Some of how that ecosystem describes itself is the ecosystem's own description. I present it that way, and check it against neutral sources where I can. Fourth, the scope. This approach suits content, dashboards and hypermedia surfaces. Rich client interactivity, offline work and very large dynamic interfaces stay genuinely harder. Fifth, symmetry has edges. Some surfaces only the AI writes to, like the narration console. The claim is symmetry of the operable vocabulary, not that every surface goes both ways.

beats.quote: That is the contribution, and it is enough.
beats.text: Should an AI operate the human interface? Largely settled, yes. The open question is how. The common answer is imitation under instruction. Mine is one closed vocabulary that a human and an AI operate identically, through one door, with the AI's hand shown in the type. In the older language of the field, the machine extends the operator's reach without leaving their sight. Authoring symmetry, action symmetry and standard channels have all shipped somewhere. None of them lets the operator see, in the surface, whose hand did what. It's a synthesis and an existence proof, not an invention. That is the contribution, and it is enough.

beats.quote: Re-vet every provenance-HCI source for retraction before it goes in.
beats.text: And one I caught the hard way. A source I had lined up on provenance was withdrawn by its own authors for a reporting error, and I dropped it. So now every provenance source gets checked for a retraction before it goes in. That's the kind of mistake I'd rather print than repeat. That closes the whitepaper. The plain-language version of the same argument, without the citations, is the note called Watch Its Hands, if you want it told the other way.

runes.quote: Positioning must be dated, not absolute.
That is the contribution, and it is enough.
Re-vet every provenance-HCI source for retraction before it goes in.

stops.trial: Take any claim you have published or posted about a tool you built. Write one honest limit next to it, with a date on it.
digest: The door, registry and grade are built and tested, and the live model covers a narrow slice.
The claim is dated, scoped and not proven to help anyone yet.
Retracted sources get checked before they go in.
